messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Speed Results
parts:
I created a wiki page to compare speed the speed models across configurations:

https://code.google.com/p/stan/wiki/SpeedResults

Unlike the test-unit results where we are fishing for bugs, here I think we only need to compare the best versions of each compiler for whatever the optimal level of optimization is (I've done O3 for now, but for me O2 is about the same for execution and somewhat faster for compilation). It would be good if someone could put some Mac results up there. Windows, too, I guess although any compiler other than the one included in Rtools is probably a headache to get working.

Note that the wiki is a separate git repo

https://code.google.com/p/stan/source/checkout?repo=wiki

And rather than using the web interface, it is probably easier to clone, edit that page with a text editor, add, commit, and push.

Ben

P.S. We have got to do something about the schools model in vol2.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Speed Results (& multivariate Matt trick)
parts: > On Dec 19, 2012, at 4:33 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
>> P.S. We have got to do something about the schools model in vol2.

I'll second that. Very cool.

I'm sort of amazed at the variation in compilers
across models. But then maybe that's random init
differences? Are they all running with the same seed?

Schools is a pretty nasty model! But there's definitely
room for both vectorization in the big data loop at the
top of the model.

And it's time to generalize the Matt trick to multivariate
models for alpha in vol2/schools/schools.stan

transformed data {
vector[3] gamma_mu;
cov_matrix[3] gamma_Sigma;
cov_matrix[3] invR;
invR <- inverse(R);
...
parameters {
...
vector[3] alpha[M];
...
model {

# Priors for random coefficients:
for (m in 1:M) alpha[m] ~ multi_normal(gamma, Sigma);

# Hyper-priors:
gamma ~ multi_normal(gamma_mu, gamma_Sigma); //
Sigma ~ inv_wishart(3, invR);

- Bob

On Thursday, December 20, 2012 2:18:35 AM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> On Dec 19, 2012, at 4:33 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
I'm sort of amazed at the variation in compilers
across models.  But then maybe that's random init
differences?  Are they all running with the same seed?

Same seed. TFC includes scarcely more than this R function

bench <- function(i) {
  mark <- "elapsed"
  compile <- system.time(fit <- stan_demo(i, chains = 0, iter = 0))[mark]
  execute <- system.time(fit <- stan_demo(i, fit = fit, seed = 12345, refresh = -1))[mark]
  if (length(dim(fit)) == 0) execute <- NA_real_ # failure
  return(c(compile, execute))
}

which is executed on each .stan file. Something could be said for increasing the number of observations so that we have fewer examples that take a tenth of a second to execute, but that would be killer for the examples that take minutes to execute.

And it's time to generalize the Matt trick to multivariate
models for alpha in vol2/schools/schools.stan

We do have stuff in the manual about that. More generally, are the bugs_examples intended to be literal translations of BUGS examples or should we be tricking them out? In a couple of cases, we have both an unvectorized and a vectorized version of the model, but that is not so helpful when the unvectorized version is unreasonably slow.

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: BUGS/JAGS models: clarity vs. speed
parts:
On 12/20/12 2:59 AM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Thursday, December 20, 2012 2:18:35 AM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:

> And it's time to generalize the Matt trick to multivariate
> models for alpha in vol2/schools/schools.stan
>
>
> We do have stuff in the manual about that. More generally, are the bugs_examples intended to be literal translations of
> BUGS examples or should we be tricking them out?

The BUGS examples are being used for both evaluation
and pedagogy.

For both purposes, we want to leave the models themselves
unchanged (I'd be OK with reparameterizations where convenient)

The JAGS versions modify the BUGS versions in
some cases. We decided ages ago to take the JAGS versions
as our basis.

For evaluation, it's clear we should do efficient
implementations.

On the pedagogy side, we have the conflicting goals
of clarity and speed.

> In a couple of cases, we have both an unvectorized and a vectorized
> version of the model, but that is not so helpful when the unvectorized version is unreasonably slow.

I see room for two versions -- one clear and one fast.

Pedagogically, that would be the best of both worlds.

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: BUGS/JAGS models: clarity vs. speed
parts:
On Friday, December 21, 2012 2:45:03 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
For evaluation, it's clear we should do efficient
implementations.

On the pedagogy side,  we have the conflicting goals
of clarity and speed.

> In a couple of cases, we have both an unvectorized and a vectorized
> version of the model, but that is not so helpful when the unvectorized version is unreasonably slow.

I see room for two versions -- one clear and one fast.

Pedagogically, that would be the best of both worlds.

It's not clear what clear entails. Or to whom, the average BUGS user or the average R user or ...? To take that model as an example

model {
  for(p in 1:N) {
     Y[p] ~ normal(alpha[school[p], 1] + alpha[school[p], 2] * LRT[p] +
                   alpha[school[p], 3] * VR[p, 1] + beta[1] * LRT[p] * LRT[p] +
                   beta[2] * VR[p, 2] + beta[3] * Gender[p] +
                   beta[4] * School_gender[p, 1] + beta[5] * School_gender[p, 2] +
                   beta[6] * School_denom[p, 1] + beta[7] * School_denom[p, 2] +
                   beta[8] * School_denom[p, 3],  exp(-.5 * (theta + phi * LRT[p])));
  }
  // min.var <- exp(-(theta + phi * (-34.6193))) # lowest LRT score = -34.6193
  // max.var <- exp(-(theta + phi * (37.3807)))  # highest LRT score = 37.3807

  # Priors for fixed effects:
  beta ~ normal(0, 100);
  // for (k in 1:8)  beta[k] ~ normal(0.0, 100);
  theta ~ normal(0.0, 100);
  phi ~ normal(0.0, 100);

  # Priors for random coefficients:

for (m in 1:M) alpha[m] ~ multi_normal(gamma, Sigma);
  # Hyper-priors:
  gamma ~ multi_normal(gamma_mu, gamma_Sigma);

Sigma ~ inv_wishart(3, invR);
}

Would it be less clear to instead do the faster

model {
  vector[N] mu;
  vector[N] sigma;
  for(p in 1:N) {
     mu[p] <- alpha[school[p], 1] + alpha[school[p], 2] * LRT[p] +
              alpha[school[p], 3] * VR[p, 1] + beta[1] * LRT[p] * LRT[p] +
              beta[2] * VR[p, 2] + beta[3] * Gender[p] +
              beta[4] * School_gender[p, 1] + beta[5] * School_gender[p, 2] +
              beta[6] * School_denom[p, 1]  + beta[7] * School_denom[p, 2] +
              beta[8] * School_denom[p, 3]; 
     sigma[p] <- exp(-.5 * (theta + phi * LRT[p]));
  }
  Y ~ normal(mu, sigma);

? To me that is no less clear, but it is certainly less BUGS-ish and more R-ish, and similarly for the vectorize vs. for loop choice

  # Priors for fixed effects:
  beta ~ normal(0, 100);
  // for (k in 1:8)  beta[k] ~ normal(0.0, 100);

I guess Matt tricking around a multi_normal or inv_wishart is both less clear, less BUGS-ish, and less R-ish.

Ben

parts:
I share your notion of clarity.

The Matt trick's clarity is probably an issue with
habit. In some ways, it's clearer to think of
a bunch of normal variates getting rescaled than to
think about drawing from all sorts of differently scaled
and located distributions.

I think having to create a vector and write into it
for vectorization is less clear for everyone.

The main reason plain old vectorization may be less
clear is that it's not immediately evident to either
the BUGS or R user how we've vectorized. That is,
we allow any of the arguments to be a scalar that's
just repeated. Most R functions won't let you do that,
will they?

- Bob

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] BUGS/JAGS models: clarity vs. speed
parts:
I don't know. It might be something as simple as that, with Bugs, the examples are in one place that's clear bounded, while with Stan, it's part of a big ugly directory including all sorts of other things. The googlecode interface is much much better than the interface in win bugs, but it looks a bit more intimidating, it's got buttons all over the place, it looks like a developer tool. Maybe people can handle it, I don't know. There's something about it that looks scary.

It's funny, here I'm taking the opposite position I take in the infovis-vs-stat-graphics debate. I'm saying that this is a superior interface for people who know what they're doing, but it's scarier for outsiders.

Given that we have the html already, I think it would be fine if it were supplemented with a pdf document that just had the R and stan code (but not the data). That way, newcomers could start out by downloading Stan, the Stan manual, and the Stan examples.

A

On 12/22/12 6:48 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> Any tex magic to avoid page breaks within braces? I'm not sure how to use the usual orphan/widow with multiline blocks.

I don't think so -- the models are all in verbatim environs.
For one, the basic paragraph marker (a blank line) isn't there.

We cold replace the verbatims with line-based things and try
to do it ourselves, but that's a bit more fine detail than I'd
like to go into. I did that for our company's manual, but it was
a pain to do all the escaping. The upside is that it let me replace
vertical lines in code with half lines and play with fonts
and things inside the code to bold pieces, etc. And also chop
down to rectangles inside of code based on comment breadcrumbs.

- Bob
